analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes to report nurse staffing levels electronically, publicly post the data, and audit it.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in August 2002 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing homes already had to post daily staffing information, but the numbers were often self-reported and hard for the public to find. This bill would have required facilities to submit the data electronically to the federal government at least quarterly, post it on a public website, include an audit of the numbers in routine inspections, and add a staffing measure to the government's public quality ratings so families could compare facilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Families choosing a nursing home for a parent or spouse, and nursing home residents, who would get verified, comparable information about how many nurses and aides were actually on duty at each facility. Understaffing is one of the strongest predictors of neglect and poor care, so accurate staffing data would give families a way to avoid poorly staffed homes before harm occurs. Nurses and aides in well-staffed facilities would also benefit from having their facilities' staffing publicly recognized.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires skilled nursing facilities and nursing facilities to submit their daily nurse staffing data electronically to the Secretary of Health and Human Services at least quarterly, with the data made publicly available on an Internet website [S3].
Adds an audit of the reported staffing data as part of each standard facility survey, so families would not be relying on unverified self-reports [S3].

Requires that the quality measures the government publishes to help the public compare nursing homes include a measure for nursing staff, showing each facility's average daily nursing hours and how it ranks against other facilities in the state [S3].
Extends the staffing-posting requirement to beds made available through hospital agreements so those beds are covered by the same transparency rules [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, who would bear the cost of quarterly electronic reporting, the added audit of their staffing records, and public disclosure of staffing levels that could reveal understaffing and affect their reputation and ability to attract residents. The Department of Health and Human Services would bear the cost of collecting, publishing, and auditing the data.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and federal regulators

drawbacks.text: Reporting and audit requirements add paperwork and compliance costs to nursing home operators, costs that for-profit facilities with thin margins would bear and could pass along [S3].

Transparency alone does not force facilities to hire more staff; publishing accurate staffing data informs families but does not itself raise minimum staffing levels or improve care in understaffed homes [S3].

The bill directs the Secretary to develop a case-mix-sensitive staffing measure but allows the agency to skip that sensitivity requirement if building the methodology would delay implementation, weakening the comparison the measure is meant to provide [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct costs are modest — electronic data submission of numbers facilities already post daily, plus an audit folded into inspections that already happen. The main benefit to families is real but indirect: better information lets people avoid badly staffed facilities, but it does not itself guarantee better staffing or care anywhere. The strongest objection is that disclosure can substitute for regulation — families can see the numbers, but nothing in the bill requires any facility to change how it staffs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in August 2002, near the end of the congressional session, and died there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley, the ranking member (and former chairman) of the Senate Finance Committee, introduced the bill on August 1, 2002, with Senators Breaux and Rockefeller [S1][S3].
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance; no further action was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
The bill had three Democratic cosponsors in the Senate, all on a committee with jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid, yet the committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators avoided quarterly electronic staffing reports, audits of their staffing data, and public rankings against other facilities in their state.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care operators
industries.note: The bill would have required quarterly electronic staffing reports, audits of those reports during routine inspections, and a public staffing ranking against other facilities in each state. Operators whose facilities are understaffed would have faced public disclosure of that fact, which is why industry groups historically prefer self-reported, hard-to-find staffing data.
Accurate, public staffing data would credit facilities that invest in nursing staff and expose those that do not, strengthening the hand of staff-to-resident ratios as a visible quality benchmark.
